meta.title: Who really said "We're Lost, But We're Making Good Time!"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yogi Berra printed it as his own in 1998 — but the gag ran in Collier's Weekly in 1947, credited to ballplayer Buddy Blattner.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We're Lost, But We're Making Good Time!'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a Yogi original: the line was a 1947 Collier's cartoon caption credited to Buddy Blattner. Berra was pinned with it by 1963.

answer.label: Not Yogi’s line — credited to Buddy Blattner, 1947
answer.authorDates: 1920–2009 · New York Giants infielder, world table-tennis champion, later a sportscaster
answer.sourceLine: The joke was already running in a national magazine in 1947: Collier’s Weekly published it on 11 October 1947 as an airline-pilot gag in a George Lichty cartoon, and in February 1948 the magazine reprinted the panel and credited the caption to New York Giants infielder Buddy Blattner. Berra did claim the line as his own in The Yogi Book (1998), dating it to a 1972 drive to the Hall of Fame — but it had been attached to him in print since 1963, and Quote Investigator ↗ concludes he was “employing a pre-existing punchline.”

source.excerpt:
Collier’s Weekly, 11 October 1947 — a George Lichty cartoon panel showing a uniformed airline pilot addressing his passengers:
“We’re still lost, but we’re making very good time!”
trail: 11 October 1947 — Collier’s Weekly runs a George Lichty cartoon of an airline pilot telling his passengers “We’re still lost, but we’re making very good time!” This is the earliest appearance known to Quote Investigator ↗.

14 February 1948 — Collier’s reprints the panel and names the writer: the gag “came from the fertile brain of Buddy Blattner, of the New York Giants, who sold it to Collier’s, who farmed it to Lichty.” Transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗

1959–1962 — the gag keeps moving: a North Carolina paper gives it to a pilot with a broken compass in 1959, Joe McCarthy’s humour column “In One Ear” in The American Weekly of 14 August 1960 has it on a Hawaii-bound airliner, and a 1962 “Laughing Matter” cartoon finally puts it in a car, spoken by a woman holding a map. Quote Investigator ↗

1963, then 1998 — Merle Jones pins a Yogi-and-Garagiola version on Berra in the Southern Illinoisan of 28 October 1963; thirty-five years on, Berra prints it in The Yogi Book (Workman, 1998), p. 51, as something he said driving to the Hall of Fame in 1972. The book is borrowable at the Internet Archive ↗, and QI verified the page on paper.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from Collier’s Weekly, 11 October 1947, p. 61. Four months later Collier’s reprinted the panel and credited the caption not to the cartoonist but to ballplayer Buddy Blattner. The car, the map and Yogi Berra all arrive later.

source.rightsHolder: The Crowell-Collier Publishing Company (Collier’s Weekly, 1947–48); Workman Publishing and the estate of Yogi Berra (The Yogi Book, 1998)
source.rightsNote: No form of this line is documented before 1947, so nothing here falls in the pre-1931 US public-domain window. The earliest known appearance is a cartoon caption in Collier’s Weekly of 11 October 1947, and the exact wording most people quote comes from The Yogi Book (Workman Publishing, 1998) — a plainly in-copyright modern book. Treat the sentence as in-copyright and use it as a short attributed quotation.

author.name: Buddy Blattner
author.heading: Who was Buddy Blattner?
author.bio: Robert Garnett ‘Buddy’ Blattner won world table-tennis doubles titles in 1936 and 1937 before playing five major-league seasons for the Cardinals, Giants and Phillies, then spent a quarter-century in the broadcast booth — calling Game of the Week alongside Dizzy Dean and later doing the Angels and the Royals. He is not remembered as a comedy writer, which is part of why this credit evaporated: when Collier’s reprinted the cartoon in February 1948, it noted that the gag had been sold to the magazine by Blattner, then a New York Giants infielder, and farmed out to the cartoonist. The punchline outlived the credit by about eighty years.

copyAttribution: "We're lost, but we're making good time!" — popularly Yogi Berra, who printed it in The Yogi Book (Workman, 1998, p. 51) as something he said on a 1972 drive to the Baseball Hall of Fame. But the gag was already in print: a George Lichty cartoon in Collier's Weekly, 11 October 1947, had an airline pilot tell his passengers "We're still lost, but we're making very good time!", and in February 1948 Collier's credited the caption to New York Giants infielder Buddy Blattner. A sports column had pinned a version on Berra by October 1963. Chronology: Quote Investigator, 11 July 2012.

misattribution.heading: Why everyone says Yogi
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-repeated Yogi-isms, and it is the rare case where Berra himself claimed the line. But the joke was already in a national magazine when he was in his second season with the Yankees, and it reached him the way stock gags always do — through a sports column.

items.who: Yogi Berra, as the line’s author
items.why: Quote sites run it flat under his name. AZQuotes ↗ credits it to Berra and sources it to The Yogi Book (1998), with nothing to indicate the gag had been in print for half a century by then.
A George Lichty cartoon panel showed a uniformed pilot telling his passengers “We’re still lost, but we’re making very good time!” This is the earliest appearance known to Quote Investigator ↗.

When Collier’s reprinted the panel on 14 February 1948, it added that the gag “came from the fertile brain of Buddy Blattner, of the New York Giants, who sold it to Collier’s, who farmed it to Lichty.” Transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗

Merle Jones ran a Yogi-and-Garagiola car version in the Southern Illinoisan on 28 October 1963 — which QI notes is “almost a decade before the date that Berra himself gave” for saying it. Quote Investigator ↗

misattribution.truthLine: It is a stock 1940s gag: first documented in Collier’s Weekly on 11 October 1947 and credited there to ballplayer Buddy Blattner. Yogi Berra told a version of it and printed it as his own in 1998 — but, as Quote Investigator ↗ puts it, he was “employing a pre-existing punchline.”

context.heading: How a cockpit joke became a Yogi-ism
lead: Yogi Berra is a quote magnet: lines drift toward him because they sound like something he would say, and because his name makes the joke land. His own 1998 book is titled I really didn’t say everything I said! — an admission, from the source, that the corpus had outgrown the man. This line is the unusual case where Berra claimed one back, printing it as something he said on a 1972 drive to the Baseball Hall of Fame with his wife Carmen and their three sons.

The trouble is that the joke was already old. Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to a George Lichty cartoon in Collier’s Weekly of 11 October 1947, in which an airline pilot tells his passengers they are still lost but making very good time — and to a February 1948 reprint where the magazine named Buddy Blattner as the caption’s author. By 1962 the setting had moved from cockpit to car, and by October 1963 a sports column had put the line in Yogi’s mouth, which QI notes is “almost a decade before the date that Berra himself gave.”
context.detailsSummary: Two Garagiola versions that don’t match
detailsBody: Joe Garagiola turns up in two different tellings and they disagree. In the 1963 Southern Illinoisan column, Yogi has just bought his first car in St. Louis and picks Joe up for a drive; Joe says “Yogi, you’re lost,” and Yogi answers “Yeah, I know it, but were making good time.” Transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗

In the October 1971 Baseball Digest, Garagiola is instead visiting Berra in New Jersey, notices they have passed the same church three times and asks “We’re lost, huh?” — to which Yogi replies “But we’re making good time, ain’t we?” Different state, different car, different decade. Quote Investigator ↗

Berra’s own 1998 account has neither Garagiola nor a church: he is driving his family to Cooperstown in 1972, and the line is aimed at Carmen — “Carmen was giving me a hard time, so I gave it back.” Three incompatible settings for one punchline is the signature of a floating joke, not a remembered remark. Quote Investigator ↗
context.pull: The gag, incidentally, came from the fertile brain of Buddy Blattner, of the New York Giants, who sold it to Collier’s, who farmed it to Lichty.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Yogi Berra, who used the line but did not coin it. Collier's Weekly credited the caption to Buddy Blattner in February 1948; that is the earliest known credit.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's article traces the joke to a George Lichty cartoon in Collier's Weekly of 11 October 1947 ('We're still lost, but we're making very good time!'), records the 14 February 1948 Collier's reprint crediting the caption to Buddy Blattner of the New York Giants, documents 1959, 1960, 1962, 1963 (Merle Jones, Southern Illinoisan, 28 Oct 1963), 1968 and 1971 (Baseball Digest, Joe Garagiola) versions, cites The Yogi Book (1998) p. 51 for Berra's 1972 Hall of Fame drive account, and concludes Berra 'may indeed have used this line, but apparently he was employing a pre-existing punchline.'
Internet Archive holds a borrowable copy of 'The Yogi book: I really didn't say everything I said!' by Yogi Berra, published New York: Workman Pub., 1998, 127 p.

Robert Garnett 'Buddy' Blattner (February 8, 1920 – September 4, 2009) was an American table tennis and professional baseball player who played for the St. Louis Cardinals (1942), New York Giants (1946–1948) and Philadelphia Phillies (1949), won world table-tennis doubles gold in 1936 and 1937, and became a radio and television sportscaster.

SABR's BioProject biography of Buddy Blattner records his 1936 and 1937 world doubles table-tennis titles, his MLB career with the Cardinals, Giants and Phillies, and his broadcasting career including Game of the Week with Dizzy Dean, the Angels and the Royals; it contains no passage describing him as a gag writer.

Lawrence Peter 'Yogi' Berra (May 12, 1925 – September 22, 2015) was a New York Yankees catcher who later managed and coached, was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1972, and was renowned for malapropisms and pithy remarks.

Wikiquote's Yogi Berra page — which has Quotes/Yogiisms, Disputed and Misattributed sections — does not contain the phrase 'making good time' anywhere; the line is listed in none of its sections. (Verified by grepping the page's raw wikitext: zero matches.)
AZQuotes presents 'We're lost, but we're making good time.' under Yogi Berra's name, sourced only to 'The Yogi Book (1998)', with no indication the gag predates him.
